transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what's been troubling you or what brings you here today?

Hello, doctor. Thank you. Yes, well, I suppose what brings me in is... it's honestly getting to the point where I just can't keep living like this. I know that sounds a bit dramatic, and I'm always telling my secondary students not to exaggerate, but it really is the truth. I've realized lately that I am entirely arranging my life, my daily routine, my own home, around just... not seeing spiders. It's completely taken over. 

For instance, the laundry. The washer and dryer are down in the unfinished part of the basement, which is perfectly normal for a house my age, but I just keep putting it off. I'll let the baskets pile up until I literally have nothing professional to wear to school, all because the thought of going down those wooden stairs and maybe seeing one in the corner or near the basin... I just can't do it. I stand at the top of the stairs and I just can't make myself go down there. 

And it's not just the basement, either. The garden shed out back is completely off-limits to me now. I used to keep everything so tidy in there, but now I won't even open the door. I even—and this is the part that really made me realize I need to talk to someone, because it's getting so expensive and frankly ridiculous—I've actually started paying people to do these tiny, simple jobs around the house. Things I know perfectly well how to do myself! Like getting the lawnmower out, or fetching a specific wrench, or clearing a gutter. But if it involves going into the shed, or going into one of those spaces where a spider might be, I just pay a handyman or a neighbor kid to do it because I physically cannot make myself go into those spaces. It's just so frustrating to be a grown woman, an educated person, and feel like I'm held hostage in my own home.

When you think about spiders, do you have repeated, intrusive thoughts or mental images that upset you, like worrying you might accidentally touch one or imagining them crawling on you even when they aren't there?

No, no, it's not really like that. I mean, I'm not sitting in my classroom while my students are taking a test, just daydreaming about spiders crawling all over me. It's not like a movie playing in my head or anything like that. I don't have these sudden flashes of them when I'm just going about my day, grading papers or cooking dinner. 

It's really only when I'm faced with a situation where I know they might be. Like, if I know I have to go down to the basement, then yes, I start thinking about them. I start picturing where they might be hiding—behind the washing machine, up in the rafters, near that little window that doesn't quite close right. But it's not like these thoughts just pop into my head out of nowhere when I'm perfectly safe in my living room. It's very specific to the places where they live. If I'm not near a place like that, or if I don't have to go near a place like that, I'm not really thinking about them at all. I'm just thinking about my lesson plans or what I need to pick up at the grocery store. So, no, I wouldn't say I have those kinds of intrusive images you're talking about, not unless I'm actively having to confront a space where I know they are.
When you're in a situation where you actually see a spider or think one might be nearby, what happens to your body or your feelings in that moment?

Well, it's... it's incredibly immediate, is the best way I can describe it. It's not something I can talk myself out of, which is so frustrating because, like I said, I'm an educated person, I'm a teacher, I know logically that a house spider in the basement isn't going to kill me. But my body just completely takes over. If I'm standing at the top of those basement stairs, and I actually spot one—even just a shadow that looks like one, or one of those awful, spindly ones in the corner—my chest just tightens up right away. It's like all the air gets sucked out of the room. 

And my hands, they start shaking so badly. The other day, I was holding a basket of towels, just trying to force myself to go down, and I saw something move near the baseboard, and my hands were trembling so much I actually dropped the basket right there on the landing. Towels everywhere. And in that moment, I either completely freeze up—like my feet are glued to the floorboards and I couldn't move if the house were on fire—or I just back out of the space so incredibly fast. It's almost like my body has made the decision to run before my brain has even fully processed what I'm looking at. I'll just slam the door shut and stand in the hallway, breathing hard, feeling so foolish but completely unable to go back in. It's a very intense, very physical reaction. It's not just a mild dislike, it's a full-body panic.

When you avoid going into places like the basement or the garden shed, is it mainly because you’re afraid of having that intense physical reaction, or is it more about trying to avoid seeing or being near a spider in the first place?

Well, I suppose... I mean, I guess it’s a bit of both, but if I’m really honest with myself, it’s mostly just the sheer terror of the spider itself. Yes, the panic is awful. It’s exhausting, truly. I hate how my heart races and how I feel like I can’t catch my breath, and I hate dropping my laundry and feeling like a complete fool in my own hallway. It’s embarrassing, even when I’m completely alone in the house. I’ll stand there afterward, leaning against the wall, just berating myself. "You’re fifty-four years old," I’ll tell myself, "You teach trigonometry to teenagers who are far more intimidating than a little bug, pull yourself together." 

But when I’m actually standing at the top of those stairs, looking down into the gloom, I’m not thinking, "Oh, I hope my heart doesn’t start racing." I’m not worried about my hands shaking. I’m thinking, "Where are they? Is there one on the handrail? Is there one in that web in the corner by the water heater?" It’s the creature itself that I can’t bear the thought of. The way they move, those awful, long, spindly legs... just the idea of one being near me, or heaven forbid, getting *on* me, or me accidentally brushing against one when I’m reaching for the detergent... that’s what keeps me from going down there. 

I’ll actually try to bargain with myself. I’ll say, "Okay, just go down three steps, grab the basket, and come right back up." But then I picture one of them scuttling out from under the bottom step, and I just... I can’t. So, while the physical reaction is terrible, and I certainly don't enjoy feeling like I'm having a heart attack over a piece of laundry, it’s really the spiders themselves that I’m avoiding. If I could somehow guarantee, with absolute one hundred percent certainty, that there wasn't a single spider in that basement, I wouldn't be afraid to go down there at all. I wouldn't worry about having a panic attack, because there would be nothing down there to trigger it. It’s the presence of the spider, or even just the *possibility* of the spider, that I’m running from.
Is your fear limited only to spiders, or do you also experience similar intense reactions to other insects or small creatures, like ants, beetles, or even images of spiders in books or on television?

Oh, no, it’s really just the spiders. Ants, beetles, bees, caterpillars... none of those bother me in the slightest. I mean, if I see a line of ants marching across the kitchen counter, I just wipe them up or set out one of those little plastic traps and I don't give it a second thought. Sometimes my students even bring in insects for their science projects, and I can walk right by the terrariums without batting an eye. So it’s definitely not a general bug thing at all. 

Now, as for pictures or television... well, I certainly don't enjoy looking at them. If I’m watching a nature documentary on PBS and suddenly there’s a massive close-up of one, I will absolutely look away or change the channel. I'll get a little shiver, certainly. But I don't freeze up or drop my laundry like I do in the hallway. I know it’s just on the screen and it can't actually get to me. 

But the real thing, in my own physical space... it's just entirely different. And it's so frustrating because I know a spider in the corner of an old house probably isn’t going to hurt me. I know the logic. I know they eat pests and they’re supposedly more afraid of us than we are of them. But the moment I picture one dropping out of a box of winter clothes, or sitting near the washer when I'm just trying to do a simple load of towels... it feels enormous and threatening in a way I’m embarrassed to admit. I mean, I'll stand there imagining it dropping onto my shoulder, or crawling over my shoe, and this tiny little creature that I could easily step on suddenly feels like a life-or-death threat. It’s completely out of proportion, I know it is, but I just can't shake that feeling of absolute, paralyzing dread. So, yes, it's just spiders, but the way they make me feel is just... so overwhelming.
